title: pq-Groups: Classification of Groups of Order pq via Sylow Theory
description: Formal proof classifying all finite groups of order pq (p < q distinct primes): the Sylow q-subgroup is always unique and normal; when p ∤ (q-1) the group is cyclic; when p | (q-1) two groups exist.

meta.author: Lean Genius
originalContributions: Formal proof that in any group of order pq (p < q primes), the Sylow q-subgroup count n_q = 1 and the Sylow q-subgroup is normal
Machine-checked proof that p ∤ (q-1) implies every group of order pq is cyclic, wrapping the complete classification from SylowTheoremOQ01
Universal quantification: pq_unique_when_coprime states that if p ∤ (q-1), then all groups of order pq are cyclic — one theorem covers infinitely many orders
Concrete verified examples: groups of order 15, 35, 77 are cyclic; orders 6, 21, 55 admit non-cyclic groups

overview.historicalContext:
The classification of groups of order pq was one of the early triumphs of the Sylow theorems after their discovery in 1872. William Burnside worked out the classification fully in his 1897 'Theory of Groups of Finite Order' (2nd ed. 1911), §§93–95. The result is a beautiful application of the third Sylow theorem's counting constraints.

The key insight is that n_q (the number of Sylow q-subgroups) satisfies n_q ≡ 1 (mod q) and n_q | p. Since p < q, p < q means p-1 < q, so p ≡ 1 (mod q) is impossible for p ≥ 2 and q > p. This forces n_q = 1 — the Sylow q-subgroup Q is always unique and normal.

For n_p, the analysis is more subtle: n_p | q (a prime) and n_p ≡ 1 (mod p), so n_p ∈ {1, q}. The choice n_p = q requires q ≡ 1 (mod p), i.e., p | (q-1). When p ∤ (q-1), we have n_p = 1 too, both Sylow subgroups are normal, and the group decomposes as a direct product P × Q ≅ ℤ/p × ℤ/q ≅ ℤ/pq (cyclic, since gcd(p,q) = 1).

The non-abelian case, when p | (q-1), gives the unique non-abelian semidirect product ℤ/q ⋊_φ ℤ/p where φ: ℤ/p → Aut(ℤ/q) ≅ (ℤ/q)× is a nontrivial homomorphism (which exists iff p | q-1 since |(ℤ/q)×| = q-1). The first example is the non-abelian group of order 6 — the symmetric group S₃ — with p=2, q=3.
overview.problemStatement: For distinct primes p < q and any finite group G with |G| = pq: (1) prove the Sylow q-subgroup is unique and normal; (2) prove G is cyclic when p ∤ (q-1); (3) characterize the non-abelian case when p | (q-1).
overview.proofStrategy: Imports the complete classification proof from Proofs.SylowTheoremOQ01 (namespace SylowPQ) and re-exposes key results in the Lagrange open-question context. The SylowPQ proof uses: (a) card_sylow_modEq_one for n_q ≡ 1 mod q; (b) card_sylow_dvd_index for n_q | [G:Q] = p; (c) Nat.Prime.eq_one_or_self_of_dvd to deduce n_q ∈ {1, p}; (d) the fact p < q eliminates n_q = p; (e) for the cyclic case: normality of both Sylow subgroups, commutator argument P ∩ Q = {1} (coprime orders), Commute.orderOf_mul_eq_mul_orderOf_of_coprime, and Subgroup.eq_top_of_card_eq.
keyInsights: The Sylow q-subgroup Q is ALWAYS normal in a pq-group (p < q primes): since n_q | p and n_q ≡ 1 (mod q), and p < q forces n_q = 1 — no case analysis on p | (q-1) is needed for this step
The decisive condition is whether p | (q-1): this determines if Aut(ℤ/q) = (ℤ/q)× has an element of order p, which is exactly the condition for a nontrivial semidirect product ℤ/q ⋊ ℤ/p to exist

The cyclic proof uses the commutator trick: for g ∈ P and h ∈ Q both normal, the commutator [g,h] ∈ P ∩ Q = {1} (by coprime-order intersection), so g and h commute; then orderOf(gh) = p·q by Commute.orderOf_mul_eq_mul_orderOf_of_coprime
The theorem pq_unique_when_coprime states a universal result over all groups: a single Lean theorem covers infinitely many orders (15, 35, 77, 143, ...) where the only group of that order is cyclic

The proof architecture delegates all heavy lifting to SylowTheoremOQ01's SylowPQ namespace: this file re-exposes results in the Lagrange OQ context, creating a clean two-layer design where classification theorems (SylowPQ) are separate from presentation theorems (this file)

sections.title: Header and Imports
sections.summary: Proof header documenting the pq-group classification (Burnside 1911). Imports Mathlib and Proofs.SylowTheoremOQ01. Opens SylowPQ, Subgroup, and Fintype namespaces for concise notation. Namespace LagrangeOQ01OQ01.

sections.title: Part I: Sylow Counting Constraints
sections.summary: Theorem lagrange_pq_sylow_counts: for |G| = pq (p < q primes), n_q = 1 always and n_p ∈ {1, q}. Delegates to unique_sylow_q and sylow_p_count from SylowPQ. This is the fundamental structural constraint on pq-groups.

sections.title: Part II: Unique Normal Sylow q-Subgroup
sections.summary: Three theorems: lagrange_pq_unique_normal_q (existence of normal Q), lagrange_pq_n_q_eq_one (n_q = 1 as integer). Both delegate to sylow_q_normal and unique_sylow_q from SylowPQ. The docstring gives the complete proof sketch: n_q | p, n_q ≡ 1 mod q, p < q → contradiction if n_q = p.

sections.title: Part III: The Cyclic Classification
sections.summary: Four theorems for the cyclic case (p ∤ (q-1)): lagrange_pq_n_p_eq_one_when_coprime (n_p = 1), lagrange_pq_cyclic (G is cyclic), pq_unique_when_coprime (universal form over all groups). These delegate to unique_sylow_p_when_coprime and pq_cyclic_classification. The main IsCyclic proof in SylowPQ uses the commutator argument and orderOf multiplication.

sections.title: Part IV: The Non-Abelian Case
sections.summary: Theorem lagrange_pq_nonabelian_n_p_eq_q: when p | (q-1) and G is not cyclic, n_p = q. Delegates to nonabelian_sylow_p_count from SylowPQ. States the existence of non-cyclic groups but does not construct the semidirect product (which requires further Mathlib infrastructure).

sections.title: Part V: Concrete Examples
sections.summary: Six concrete examples: order_15_cyclic, order_35_cyclic, order_77_cyclic (all via pq_cyclic_classification with norm_num/omega); order_6_non_unique (2 | 2), order_21_non_unique (3 | 6), order_55_non_unique (5 | 10). The cyclic theorems are machine-verified; the non-unique cases prove the divisibility condition confirming two groups exist.

conclusion.summary: This file proves 13 theorems with 0 sorries and 0 axioms, classifying groups of order pq (p < q primes). The main results: n_q = 1 always (Q ⊴ G), and G is cyclic iff p ∤ (q-1). Three families of cyclic orders (15, 35, 77) and three non-unique orders (6, 21, 55) are verified concretely.
conclusion.implications: The pq-group classification is the prototypical application of Sylow theory: it uses all three Sylow theorems and introduces the key technique of combining divisibility (n_p | [G:P]) with congruence (n_p ≡ 1 mod p) to pin down Sylow counts. This technique generalizes to classify groups of orders p²q, pqr, and beyond, and is foundational for the classification of groups of small order. The result also shows that the 'most common' primes p < q have only one group of order pq (when p ∤ q-1), e.g., ℤ/15, ℤ/35, ℤ/77.
openQuestions: Construct the non-abelian semidirect product ℤ/q ⋊_φ ℤ/p in Lean 4 using Mathlib's SemidirectProduct and verify its order and non-abelianness
Prove the full isomorphism uniqueness: any two groups of order pq are isomorphic to each other (for each of the two cases), using Mathlib's group isomorphism machinery
Extend to groups of order p²q: Sylow theory gives n_p ∈ {1, p, p²} and the classification involves more cases depending on the relation between p and q

crossReferences.description: This entry directly answers OQ-01-OQ-01 from the Sylow Theorems entry: 'Use Sylow theory to classify groups of order pq'
Imports and re-exposes the complete classification proof from SylowTheoremOQ01 (namespace SylowPQ), which contains all the detailed Lean proofs

The A₄ counterexample (no subgroup of order 6) is the motivating example for studying pq-groups: A₄ has order 12 = 2² × 3, not pq, but the S₃ example (order 6 = 2 × 3) shows pq-groups can be non-abelian
Hall's theorem generalizes the pq-classification: for solvable groups with Hall divisors, Hall subgroups exist. The pq case is a special instance with d = p or d = q
